newsitem.title: DUBAI: Americans in Saudi not alarmed by new warning.
newsitem.headline: Americans in Saudi not alarmed by new warning.

text.p: Americans living in Saudi Arabia kept to their daily routines on Wednesday saying they were concerned but not alarmed by a new warning of possible attacks on U.S. interests in the kingdom.

In the latest warning, the U.S. embassy on Tuesday told Americans in the kingdom that "planning for terrorist action against U.S. interests in Saudi Arabia continues unabated" following new threats by a leading Islamist dissident.

Americans reached by telephone in the Saudi capital Riyadh said they had been living under tight security precautions since the attack on a U.S. military training centre in Riyadh in November 1995 which killed five Americans and two Indians.

Security at the U.S. embassy and consulates as well as residential compounds housing most of the 35,000 U.S. citizens in the kingdom was stepped up following the June bombing which killed 19 servicemen in the eastern province.

Western diplomats said that since the June bombing the 5,000 U.S. troops in Saudi Arabia have been put on the highest possible threat alert with instructions to prepare as though another attack against them were imminent.
"They are definitely more prepared than before and are certainly not letting their guard down," one said.
Since June the embassy has issued six warnings of possible attacks and urged Americans to keep a low profile.
"The new warning does not tell us anything new. We are already cautious and I cannot think what other precautions we can take," said one U.S. engineer in Riyadh.

The new warning followed threats by Saudi-born financier Osama bin Ladin that he would wage an Islamic holy war against the United States and its allies unless Washington removed its troops from the Gulf region.
The U.S. embassy in Riyadh refused to comment on any new security measures and would not say if it was receiving any inquiries from concerned Americans.
"Every time the embassy issues a warning we are concerned, but it has kind of become part of life here," said an American woman whose children go to the American school in Riyadh.
